concepts.name: Prahar System: Division of Day into Time Cycles
key_dimensions: Division of 24-hour day into 8 prahars of 3 hours each and their boundaries
Distinction between Poorvanga (first half) and Uttaranga (second half) prahars and their melodic characteristics
Relationship between Vadi-Samvadi swaras and prahar assignment rules
UPSC trap: confusion between prahar numbering in Hindustani vs. conceptual time slots

concepts.name: Vadi-Samvadi Rule for Time Determination
key_dimensions: Rule that ragas with Vadi in Poorvanga (Sa to Pa) are sung in first half of day/night; Uttaranga Vadi in second half
Exceptions to the Vadi-Samvadi rule (e.g., Bhairav family ragas sung at dawn despite Vadi in Uttaranga)
How Vadi-Samvadi relationship mirrors the 4th-5th interval (Madhyam-Pancham symmetry)
UPSC trap: conflating Vadi with the most frequent note rather than the most important note

concepts.name: Sandhi Prakash Ragas: Junction Ragas at Dawn and Dusk
key_dimensions: Definition of Sandhi Prakash as the transitional twilight period and its two occurrences (dawn/dusk)
Characteristic use of both Komal Re and Komal Dha (flat 2nd and flat 6th) defining this raga family
Key ragas: Bhairav (dawn), Puriya Dhanashri, Marwa, Poorvi (dusk) and their distinguishing features
UPSC trap: Bhairav is a dawn raga but Bhairavi (similar name) is an 'any time' raga — a classic name-confusion trap

concepts.name: Ritu (Seasonal) Ragas: The Six-Season Framework
key_dimensions: Six Indian seasons (Ritu): Vasant, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemant, Shishir and their approximate calendar months
Canonical seasonal ragas: Bahar/Hindol (Vasant), Miyan Malhar (Varsha), Deepak (Grishma)
Natyashastra and Sangita Ratnakara as earliest textual sources associating ragas with seasons
UPSC trap: multiple ragas can share one season; examinees must know the primary/canonical association

concepts.name: Malhar Raga Family and the Monsoon Association
key_dimensions: Malhar as the archetype monsoon raga family — Miyan ki Malhar, Gaud Malhar, Megh Malhar, Ramdasi Malhar
Tansen's contribution: Miyan ki Malhar attributed to Tansen and legend of invoking rain
Megh Malhar as distinct from Miyan ki Malhar — different swara structure despite same seasonal association
UPSC trap: 'Megh' (cloud) raga is not the same as 'Megh Malhar'; also Malhar ≠ only one raga

concepts.name: Bhairav Thaat and Dawn Ragas: Structure and Derivatives
key_dimensions: Bhairav thaat structure: Komal Re, Komal Dha with all other swaras shuddha — and its dawn-time prescription
Major ragas derived from Bhairav thaat: Bhairav, Ahir Bhairav, Ramkali, Vibhas, Kalingra
Ahir Bhairav as a post-dawn raga (late morning) versus pure Bhairav at exact dawn — temporal nuance
UPSC trap: Bhairav is both a raga AND a thaat — examinees confuse the two distinct entities

concepts.name: Night Ragas: First and Second Half Distinction
key_dimensions: First half of night ragas (9 PM–12 AM): Yaman, Kedar, Hameer, Kalyan thaat group
Second half of night ragas (12 AM–3 AM): Darbari Kanada, Bageshri, Bhimpalasi (late night)
Yaman as the archetypal early evening raga — teevra Madhyam as its defining feature
UPSC trap: Bhimpalasi is a late afternoon raga, not night — examinees confuse its somber mood with night

concepts.name: Kalyan Thaat Ragas and the Evening Time Slot
key_dimensions: Kalyan thaat: only Teevra (sharp) Madhyam, all other shuddha — associated with early evening (6–9 PM)
Key ragas: Yaman, Yaman Kalyan, Shyam Kalyan, Shuddha Kalyan — their subtle distinctions
Yaman vs. Yaman Kalyan: use of both Teevra and Shuddha Madhyam in Yaman Kalyan as the key difference
UPSC trap: Kalyan is a thaat AND a raga (Shuddha Kalyan) — same name confusion as Bhairav

concepts.name: Hindol Raga: Spring and Morning Association
key_dimensions: Hindol as a pentatonic (audava) raga — omits Re and Pa, creating unique spring-morning mood
Associated with Vasant Ritu (spring) AND early morning — dual time-season association
Hindol in Carnatic tradition vs. Hindol in Hindustani — different structure, same name (classic UPSC trap)
Philosophical and devotional context: associated with Lord Krishna and the Holi festival

concepts.name: Deepak Raga: The Fire/Summer Raga and the Tansen Legend
key_dimensions: Deepak associated with Grishma (summer) and conceptually with fire — Teevra swaras creating heat mood
Legend of Tansen singing Deepak and lamps lighting spontaneously, countered by Megh Malhar for rain
Deepak's near-extinct status in contemporary practice — important for cultural heritage questions
UPSC trap: Deepak is often paired with Malhar in legend questions; examinees must identify which invokes fire vs. rain

concepts.name: Bhairavi: The 'Any Time' or 'Concluding' Raga — Exception to Time Rules
key_dimensions: Bhairavi classified as 'Sadabahaar' (evergreen/any time) raga — major exception to the prahar system
Structural basis: uses all five Komal (flat) swaras making it emotionally universal (Karuna, Shringara rasa)
Tradition of concluding a concert with Bhairavi — cultural practice and its rationale
UPSC trap: Bhairavi ≠ Bhairav; Bhairav is strictly dawn; Bhairavi transcends time — the most tested name-pair

concepts.name: Ragas and the Navarasa Connection to Time/Season
key_dimensions: Correspondence between the nine rasas and temporal-seasonal prescriptions (Shringar→spring/evening; Karuna→late night)
Bharata's Natyashastra as foundational text linking rasa theory to musical mood and appropriate performance context
How Komal swaras create Karuna/Bhakti rasa (night/late night) vs. Teevra swaras creating Veera/Raudra (afternoon)
UPSC trap: rasa determines time association in theory but multiple ragas share same rasa — examinees over-simplify

concepts.name: Afternoon Ragas: Todi and Multani — Shared Time Slot, Different Structures
key_dimensions: Todi thaat ragas prescribed for late morning to afternoon (around 12 PM–3 PM): Miyan ki Todi, Multani, Gurjari Todi
Todi vs. Multani: both afternoon, but Multani uses Teevra Madhyam while Todi uses Shuddha Madhyam — key distinction
Komal Re, Komal Ga, Komal Dha in Todi thaat creating the contemplative afternoon mood
UPSC trap: Todi and Bhairavi both use Komal Ga and Komal Dha — examinees confuse their time associations

concepts.name: Kafi Thaat Ragas and the Spring/Holi Association
key_dimensions: Kafi thaat: Komal Ga and Komal Ni — associated with spring (Vasant) and Holi festival context
Key Kafi thaat ragas: Kafi, Bageshri, Bhimpalasi, Pilu — their individual time prescriptions within the thaat
Dhrupad and Thumri traditions preferentially using Kafi thaat for Holi compositions (Dhamar tala connection)
UPSC trap: Bageshri is a late-night raga despite being in Kafi thaat — thaat does not determine time alone

concepts.name: Carnatic vs. Hindustani Systems of Raga-Time Association
key_dimensions: Hindustani system: strict prahar-based time theory; Carnatic system: less rigid but has concept of 'Sandhyakala' ragas
Carnatic ragas like Bhairavi (Sindhu Bhairavi), Todi (Shubhapantuvarali) — same mood, different structural rules for time
72 Melakarta system in Carnatic: time association less codified than Hindustani 10-thaat system
UPSC trap: ragas with similar names (Bhairav/Mayamalavagowla; Yaman/Kalyani) are NOT the same across traditions

concepts.name: Historical Evolution of Raga-Time Theory: From Natyashastra to Modern Practice
key_dimensions: Natyashastra (Bharata, ~200 BCE–200 CE): earliest systematic reference to grama, murchhana — precursor to time theory
Sangita Ratnakara (Sarangadeva, 13th century): first detailed classification of ragas by time and season
Man Kautuhal (Tansen's period, 16th century) and Mughal court's role in crystallizing time-raga associations
UPSC trap: time theory is a medieval development — it is NOT present in Vedic or early classical texts as a systematic code

concepts.name: Raga-Ragini System vs. Thaat System: Impact on Time Classification
key_dimensions: Raga-Ragini system (medieval): 6 male ragas (Bhairav, Malkauns, Hindol, Deepak, Megh, Shri) each with 5 raginis — time-based family trees
Pandit Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande's 10-Thaat system (20th century): reorganized ragas by swara structure, not time
Conflict: same raga placed in different families by Hanuman Mat vs. Shiva Mat — creating time-association ambiguity
UPSC trap: the 6 'parent ragas' of the Raga-Ragini system are frequently tested; Malkauns and Shri are often confused

concepts.name: Malkauns (Malkosh): Midnight Raga and Pentatonic Structure
key_dimensions: Malkauns as a strictly midnight raga (12 AM–3 AM) — one of the most clearly time-prescribed ragas
Pentatonic (audava) structure: omits Re and Pa, uses Komal Ga, Komal Dha, Komal Ni — creating deep introspection
One of the six 'parent ragas' in the Raga-Ragini system — its historical-theoretical importance
UPSC trap: Malkauns and Darbari Kanada are both midnight/late night — but Darbari uses all seven notes (sampurna)

concepts.name: Shri Raga: Twilight-to-Evening Transition and Its Distinctive Features
key_dimensions: Shri raga prescribed for dusk (Sandhya) — one of the six parent ragas in Raga-Ragini classification
Uses both Teevra Madhyam and Komal Re — creating a rare combination that defines its emotional gravity
Shri raga's prominence in Dhrupad tradition and its near-absence in lighter classical forms
UPSC trap: Shri raga is a dusk raga like Marwa/Poorvi, but has a very different swara set — examinees group all dusk ragas together incorrectly

concepts.name: Tansen's Raga Contributions and the Court-Music Time Discipline
key_dimensions: Tansen's attributed ragas: Miyan ki Malhar, Miyan ki Todi, Darbari Kanada, Miyan ki Sarang — each with specific time slots
Akbar's court as the institutional context that formalized performance time-discipline for ragas
Darbari Kanada: late-night raga, uses Andolan (oscillation) on Komal Ga — specific performance technique linked to time mood
UPSC trap: 'Miyan ki' prefix signifies Tansen's authorship — examinees must distinguish these from the parent ragas they are derived from
